rounds.text: RBZ Jewellers Ltd trades at a remarkably low trailing P/E of 10.3x to 10.54x, sitting at a staggering discount to the broader sector benchmark of 68.18x [E1, E6]. This valuation disconnect is further underscored by a discounted cash flow intrinsic value estimate of Rs 561 per share against a market price of Rs 141, implying a substantial margin of safety of 74.9% [E39, E40]. Fundamental operating performance strongly supports this multiple expansion potential, with compounded sales growth reaching 43% over 5 years and 30% over 3 years, alongside a 42% compounded profit growth over the same 5-year period [E14, E15, E17]. Furthermore, profitability metrics outshine the industry, boasting an ROE of 18.28% to 20.1% and an ROCE of 18.74% to 21.8%, easily beating sector benchmarks [E9, E10, E12, E13]. Management's growth trajectory is robust, backed by revenue guidance of INR800 crores to INR900 crores for FY27 and strategic retail expansions in key Gujarat markets like Surat and Rajkot targeted to commence operations by Q2 FY27 [E68, E74]. Conceded: the company currently pays a dividend yield of 0.00% and reported a negative operating cash flow of Rs -7 Cr alongside a free cash flow of Rs -40 Cr in Mar 2026 [E4, E29, E30].

Despite headline growth figures, RBZ Jewellers Ltd exhibits severe cash flow degradation, evidenced by an operating cash flow of Rs -7 Cr and a free cash flow of Rs -40 Cr in March 2026, translating to a dismal cash conversion ratio of -0.13x [E28, E30]. This cash burn is accompanied by a massive surge in borrowings, which jumped nearly 87% from Rs 91 Cr to Rs 170 Cr within a single year [E33], while capital work-in-progress escalated by 733.3% to Rs 25 Cr [E34]. Furthermore, institutional backing has completely evaporated, with foreign institutional holdings collapsing from 4.33% to 0.03% and domestic holdings dropping from 3.03% to 0.01% since December 2003 [E36, E37], signaling an active institutional exit [E38]. Compounding these vulnerabilities, the company provides a zero dividend yield [E4] and suffers from high annualised volatility of 58.8% alongside a historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -57.4% [E47, E48]. Conceded: the company demonstrates strong historical profit growth [E53], an attractive headline P/E ratio [E1], and optimistic near-term revenue guidance from management [E67].

Conceded: operating cash flow was Rs -7 Cr and free cash flow was Rs -40 Cr in March 2026, leading to a negative cash conversion of -0.13x [E28, E30]. However, the sharp increase in borrowings to Rs 170 Cr and capital work-in-progress surging by 733.3% to Rs 25 Cr reflect an active capex and growth spend phase underway, supported by strong revenue guidance of INR800 crores to INR900 crores for FY27 [E33, E34, E68]. While institutional holdings have dropped, promoter holding remains rock-solid at 75.00% [E35, E36, E37]. Furthermore, the company trades at an exceptionally low P/E of 10.3x to 10.54x against a sector benchmark of 68.18x, alongside robust ROE of 18.28% to 20.1% and ROCE of 18.74% to 21.8%, vastly outperforming sector median returns [E1, E2, E6, E9, E10, E12, E13, E66]. Conceded: the dividend yield is 0.00% and historical volatility and drawdowns are high [E4, E47, E48], but this is a high-growth business delivering 42% 5-year profit CAGR and trading at a massive disconnect from its intrinsic valuation [E17, E39, E40].

Conceded: the company trades at a low P/E multiple relative to the broader sector benchmark [E1, E6]. However, pointing to headline multiples ignores severe liquidity and capital allocation flaws, specifically negative operating cash flow of Rs -7 Cr and a free cash flow deficit of Rs -40 Cr in March 2026 [E28, E30]. While the bull excuses these deficits as a natural consequence of aggressive growth spending and a 733.3% surge in capital work-in-progress [E34], this cash burn coincides with a worrying 86% expansion in borrowings to Rs 170 Cr [E33] and a simultaneous 12% year-on-year contraction in wholesale revenue [E83]. Conceded: promoter holdings remain stable at 75.00% [E35], but institutional confidence has completely evaporated with foreign and domestic institutional holdings collapsing down to near-zero levels of 0.03% and 0.01% respectively [E36, E37], driving negative institutional money flow [E38]. Finally, retail investors must endure a 0.00% dividend yield [E4] alongside high annualised volatility of 58.8% and a punishing historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -57.4% [E47, E48], proving that this low valuation is justified by acute cash flow deterioration and a complete absence of institutional backing.
